title: Area IX review: Performance and Ground Reference Maneuvers
intro: These questions mix the six Tasks of Area IX: steep turns, the steep spiral, chandelles, lazy eights, ground reference maneuvers and eights on pylons. Many join two of them in one instructing moment, such as a steep turn flown in a strong wind, rudder habits carried from chandelles into a spiral, overbanking at the slow top of a lazy eight, or a learner who flies eights on pylons like turns around a point.

questions.q: A gusty 20-knot west wind blows over the practice area. After a right steep turn your commercial learner says, 'Over the ground the circle drifted east, so next time I'll steepen the bank headed downwind, like turns around a point.' What do you teach?
options: Good idea: any turn flown in a practice area should hold a constant radius over the ground, so varying the bank with groundspeed is part of the steep turn standard too
Steepen it only on the downwind half and shallow it on the upwind half, keeping the average near 50°, because the ACS checks the average bank over the full circle
Keep the bank constant near 50°: a steep turn is flown against the horizon and graded on altitude, airspeed, bank and rollout heading, so drift is expected
Fly the turn into the wind only, because a steep turn started downwind overbanks as the groundspeed builds and has to be stopped by rolling out early
questions.why: The steep turn trains smooth, coordinated control and orientation to outside references [[24:210|AFH 10-1]], and the CFI standard is entry altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, bank ±5° and rollout on the entry heading ±10° (ACS AI.IX.A.S5). Nothing in it asks for a ground track. A constant-bank turn in wind is never a circle over the ground, even though through the air it is a perfect one [[24:150|AFH 7-4]]; varying the bank with groundspeed is the ground reference technique [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]. Changing the bank on purpose would commit a listed steep turn error, failure to maintain constant bank angle [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. Overbanking comes from the outside wing flying faster in a steep bank, not from groundspeed [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

questions.q: Your private learner trims nose-up and adds power as the bank passes 30°, flies a tidy 360° at 50°, then rolls out on heading and climbs from 3,500 to 3,620 feet as the speed drops. What happened, and what is the fix?
options: Pitch and trim on the rollout: the back pressure, nose-up trim and added power were left in; ease all three off during the rollout, with forward pressure until retrimmed
A coordination error: too much rudder on the rollout yawed the nose up, so she should keep her feet still during every rollout and let the airplane settle on its own
Nothing to fix: the altitude tolerance applies only while the airplane is banked, so a climb that begins after the wings are level is not graded in this Task
Trim is never allowed in a steep turn because the certification standards prohibit it, so she should hold all the back pressure by hand and leave the power alone
questions.why: 3,620 - 3,500 = 120 feet, past the ±100-foot entry altitude tolerance (ACS AI.IX.A.S5). The AFH lets the instructor and learner decide whether to trim, since certification standards set no trim requirement, but if trim is used both the trim and the power must be removed as the maneuver ends [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. During the rollout, back pressure, trim and power are reduced gradually to hold altitude and airspeed [[24:212|AFH 10-3]], and forward pressure may be needed until the trim is reset [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. Inadequate pitch control on rollout and ineffective use of trim are both listed errors [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. The 'never trim' option is wrong: the standards are silent on trim, not against it.

questions.q: Your commercial learner flies her first 720° steep turns both ways in bumpy afternoon air. Afterward she goes quiet and pale, says she feels a little queasy, and asks to press on to the chandelle introduction you planned. What do you do?
options: Press on with the chandelles but fly them yourself, so she can rest while still watching the maneuver she came to learn
End the lesson and head home: the AIH says an instructional flight should end as soon as incipient airsickness appears
Stay in the area and fly more steep turns at a gentler 30° bank until the queasiness passes, since the 50° bank alone caused it
Press on with the chandelles as planned, because a learner builds resistance to airsickness only by flying through the symptoms
questions.why: The AIH is direct: an instructional flight should be ended as soon as incipient airsickness appears, and rough air and abrupt maneuvers raise the odds of it [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]. A first steep turn session also brings higher G-forces and yaw felt as motion toward and away from the earth, which can confuse a pilot at first [[24:211|AFH 10-2]], so bumpy 720s fit the picture. Pressing on, whether she flies or you do, breaks that rule, and the 30° option is wrong too: the rough air is part of the cause and the sickness has already started.

questions.q: Today's plan is steep turns, then chandelles, over farmland at 1,200 feet MSL. Your learner plans the steep turns at 2,000 feet MSL 'because the ACS sets no floor for them' and the chandelles from 2,500 feet MSL. What do you say?
options: Both plans are fine: neither Task names a floor, so any altitude that keeps the airplane 500 feet above the surface meets both the ACS and the AIH guidance
Raise both: 800 feet AGL leaves too little room to recover from a nose-low bank or a stall, and the chandelles must stay at or above 2,700 feet MSL, 1,500 feet AGL
Only the steep turns are too low, because the CFI ACS sets a 1,500-foot AGL floor for steep turns but leaves the chandelle altitude to the instructor's judgment
Only the chandelles need changing, and only to 2,600 feet MSL, because the chandelle floor is measured at the 180° point, which is always higher than the entry
questions.why: The chandelle floor is in the ACS: select an altitude that allows the maneuver to be performed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.C.S2). 1,200 + 1,500 = 2,700 feet MSL; the planned 2,500 feet MSL is only 1,300 feet AGL. The steep turn Task gives no minimum altitude, but the AIH warns against teaching at an inappropriate altitude that leaves too little room to recover [[25:192|AIH 10-8]], and a nose-low steep bank can lose a significant amount of altitude in a very short time [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]; 2,000 feet MSL is only 800 feet AGL. The 2,600-foot option fails twice: it is still under 1,500 feet AGL, and a chandelle may start from a shallow dive, so the entry is not a safe place to measure from [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

questions.q: Your commercial learner flew turns around a point well last week. Before her first steep spiral she asks, 'Is my bank limit still 45°?' What is the accurate answer?
options: Yes: 45° is the ACS limit for every maneuver flown around a ground point, so the steepest downwind bank in the spiral must also stay at or below 45°
No: the spiral allows up to 60° at the steepest point; 45° is the AFH's general note for ground reference maneuvers, not an ACS limit for that Task
No: the spiral has no bank limit, because with the throttle at idle the load factor stays near 1 G whatever bank is used on the downwind side
Yes, but only below 3,000 feet AGL; above that the ACS raises the spiral limit to 60° so the learner has room to recover from an overbank
questions.why: The AFH says the steepest bank in the steep spiral should not exceed 60° [[24:213|AFH 10-4]], and the ACS reads 'not to exceed 60° angle of bank' (ACS AI.IX.B.S3). The 45° figure is the AFH's general note that a ground reference maneuver should not exceed 45° of bank or maneuvering speed [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]; the ground reference Task itself sets no ACS bank limit. Idle power does not remove the steep-bank danger: the PHAK lists accidental stalls from increased load factor in a steep turn or spiral [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]], and stall speed rises with load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. No source ties the spiral's bank limit to altitude; the altitude rule is the 1,500-foot AGL finish (ACS AI.IX.B.S6).

questions.q: After a morning of chandelles with steadily growing right rudder, your learner flies a steep spiral at idle with the same right rudder held in, and the ball sits off center all the way around. What do you teach about rudder in the spiral?
options: Hold even more right rudder than in the chandelle, because at idle the left-turning tendencies are at their strongest with the airspeed low and the propeller slow
Hold the rudder fixed where it was at the entry, because the spiral's bank keeps changing and any rudder change would stretch the circle over the ground
Use right rudder on the downwind half and left rudder on the upwind half, because a tailwind yaws the nose one way and a headwind yaws it the other way
Expect light rudder forces and maybe slight left rudder: the design compensation for P-factor and slipstream stays in a glide, while those effects are gone
questions.why: In a chandelle, right rudder is increased as the airspeed falls at high power because P-factor and other left-turning tendencies grow [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. A glide is the opposite case: the design compensation for P-factor and slipstream remains while those effects disappear, so slight left rudder is likely needed to stay coordinated [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Rudder forces are also lighter in a gliding turn, and a learner who carries over powered-flight pressures can slip or skid [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Wind changes the track over the ground, moving the airplane sideways at the wind's speed whatever its airspeed [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]; it is not a rudder input, so the downwind and upwind rudder option is wrong. Holding the rudder fixed is wrong too: the ball, not a fixed pedal, shows coordination [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

questions.q: Your learner uses the steep turn rule, a lead of half the bank, for her spiral rollout. Today the assigned heading comes up on the downwind side at 55° of bank, so she leads by about 27°, and she rolls out 15° short of it. What do you teach?
options: Half the bank is only a starting rule; the lead depends on the type of turn, the turn rate and the rollout rate, so she must judge it from the actual bank and turn rate
The rule was right, but every spiral rollout must be made on the upwind side, where the AFH requires the bank to be at its shallowest before the wings come level
Use a fixed 10° lead for every spiral whatever the bank, because the ACS heading tolerance is ±10° and a 10° lead keeps her inside it on every lap
Add the wind correction angle to half the bank, because the heading leads the position on the downwind side, then roll out as fast as she can to save altitude
questions.why: Half of 55° is 27.5°, and finishing 15° short fails the ±10° rollout tolerance (ACS AI.IX.B.S6); not completing the turn on the designated heading is a listed spiral error [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. The half-bank lead is the steep turn rule [[24:212|AFH 10-3]], and the AIH calls it a good rule of thumb for initial training, adding that the lead really depends on the type of turn, turn rate and roll-out rate [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. The spiral text gives no lead at all, only a rollout toward an object or heading into a wings-level glide with no change in airspeed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]], so the learner judges it from what the airplane is doing. Rolling out into the wind is offered as a harder variation, not a requirement [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

questions.q: On a simulated engine failure at 5,500 feet AGL, your learner flies straight ahead for two minutes comparing fields, then picks one far behind him and starts a long glide toward it. What does the AFH warn about, and where does the steep spiral fit?
options: No warning is needed: with that much altitude the best plan is to glide straight until the field is directly below, then slip off the extra height on final
He should have spiraled at once over the nearest road at 60° and the maximum allowable airspeed, because losing height fast matters more than the field
High altitude tempts a pilot to delay the decision and invites glide estimate errors; pick a field early, then descend over it to the key position
Spirals belong only in real emergencies, because the AFH says a constant gliding speed cannot be held in a turn once the throttle is closed
questions.why: The AFH warns that with the greater choice of fields at higher altitudes an inexperienced pilot may delay the decision, and with altitude to spare, errors in maneuvering and glide estimates develop [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. Once a field is chosen, the pilot may use any mix of gliding maneuvers, from wings level to spirals, to arrive at the normal key position at traffic pattern altitude [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. That is what the steep spiral trains: losing a lot of altitude while staying over a selected spot, useful in an emergency landing [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. The spiral is flown at a constant gliding speed, not a maximum speed; the steep spiral and the emergency descent usually differ in airspeed and configuration [[24:212|AFH 10-3]] [[24:213|AFH 10-4]], and holding that speed in the turns is the skill to build [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

questions.q: Your commercial learner's first chandelle in a complex airplane with a constant-speed propeller: the gear is still down from the last pattern, flaps up, and his plan is 'throttle full forward, then the prop.' What do you correct before entry?
options: Gear up first, then set the power the AFH and POH call for, normal cruise or climb, advancing the propeller control before the throttle
Leave the gear down for drag so the speed decays to just above the stall sooner, and set full throttle first, since the propeller control always follows the power
Nothing needs to change: the AFH requires full power, and the gear position does not matter, because a chandelle is judged only on the altitude gained
Gear up, then pull the propeller to its lowest rpm before the entry, because the AFH limits the chandelle to the rpm that a fixed-pitch propeller could reach
questions.why: Flaps and retractable gear should be up before the chandelle [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. With a constant-speed propeller the power may be set at normal cruise or climb as appropriate [[24:214|AFH 10-5]], and on airplanes with a controllable-pitch propeller the propeller control is advanced before engine power is increased [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. Figure 10-3 says full power while the AFH text says the recommended setting, so teach the POH setting and say which one you use [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. The chandelle is not judged on altitude gained but on how well climb performance is maximized for the power and bank chosen [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. The rpm limit applies to fixed-pitch propellers, where the throttle is set so as not to exceed it [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

questions.q: Fresh from chandelles, your learner says, 'Lazy eights end the same way: wings level at the 180° point, just above the stall.' How do the two maneuvers really differ in airspeed?
options: They are the same: both reach their slowest speed exactly at the 180° point and hold it there for a moment before the nose is lowered for the recovery
The lazy eight is slowest at 135°, its lowest pitch, and the chandelle is slowest at 90°, its highest pitch, so both are back to entry speed at 180°
A chandelle ends at 180° just above the power-on stall; a lazy eight is slowest at 90°, about 5 to 10 knots above stall, and back at entry speed at 180°
The chandelle ends at 180° at its entry airspeed, while the lazy eight ends each 180° just above stall speed, held there briefly before the next loop starts
questions.why: At the end of a chandelle the wings are level at 180°, the airspeed just above the power-on stall speed, and the nose-high attitude is held momentarily [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] (ACS AI.IX.C.S7). In a lazy eight the airspeed is at its minimum, about 5 to 10 knots above stall, at the 90° point, where the pitch passes through level and the bank is about 30° [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. At 135° the pitch is lowest and the speed is increasing, and the wings and nose come level at the original airspeed just as the 180° point is reached [[24:216|AFH 10-7]], which the ACS checks as ±10 knots from entry airspeed (ACS AI.IX.D.S5d). Then the next climbing turn starts at once, with no hold.

questions.q: Fresh from steep turns, where back pressure and power go in as the bank passes about 30°, your learner starts her first chandelle by rolling and pulling at the same time, so the nose is already well up before the bank reaches 30°. What sequence does the AFH call for?
options: Roll smoothly to about 30° first; once the bank is set, start back pressure at a constant rate while adding power, so the highest pitch comes at the 90° point
Keep the steep turn habit: add back pressure and power together as the bank goes in, since both maneuvers need the extra lift before the bank passes 30°, so start them at once
Pull up to the full pitch attitude first with the wings level, then roll in, so the climb starts as early as possible and the bank follows
Set climb power and the full pitch first, then roll to 45° at the 90° point so the turn is finished before the airspeed runs out
questions.why: In the AFH chandelle, once the entry airspeed is set the pilot enters a coordinated turn to the desired bank, generally 30°; once the bank is established, the climbing turn starts with back pressure at a constant rate while power is increased [[24:214|AFH 10-5]], timed so maximum pitch-up comes at the end of the first 90° [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. The ACS lists the same order: bank at approximately 30° (ACS AI.IX.C.S4), then power and pitch together to the 90° point with a constant bank (ACS AI.IX.C.S5). The steep turn habit does not carry over: there back pressure and power go in as the bank is being set, generally before 30° [[24:211|AFH 10-2]], because the aim is level flight. Pitch set too high can stall the airplane before the maneuver is complete [[24:213|AFH 10-4]], and a steep bank is a listed error that fails to get maximum performance [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

questions.q: As your learner, the examiner flies a left chandelle that gains only about 250 feet but ends on the 180° point just above the stall, holds it a moment and recovers smoothly. Next comes a lazy eight whose first 180° point is on heading and on entry airspeed but 150 feet above the entry altitude. Which falls outside its ACS standard?
options: Only the chandelle: 250 feet is too little gain for a maximum performance climb, while a lazy eight may gain altitude freely
Only the lazy eight: altitude at the 180° point must be within ±100 feet of entry, while the chandelle has no altitude-gain standard
Both: each must end within ±100 feet of a target altitude, the entry altitude for the lazy eight and the planned gain for the chandelle
Neither: the lazy eight's altitude is checked only after the full eight is complete, and the chandelle is graded on heading alone
questions.why: The lazy eight standard includes altitude at the 180° point ±100 feet from entry altitude (ACS AI.IX.D.S5c); 150 feet high is 50 feet outside. The chandelle elements give the 1,500-foot AGL floor, about 30° of bank and a rollout at the 180° point ±10° just above a stall airspeed, held momentarily (ACS AI.IX.C.S2, S4, S7), but no altitude gain, and the AFH judges a chandelle not by the altitude gained but by how well climb performance is maximized for the power and bank selected [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. In the lazy eight, excess power for the bank used gains altitude at the end of the maneuver, and gain or loss of altitude at each 180° point is a listed error [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

questions.q: In chandelles your learner learned to hold the 30° bank with a little opposite aileron as the speed decayed. In lazy eights he keeps the ailerons neutral at the top 'because 30° is a medium bank, and medium banks hold themselves,' and the bank creeps past 30° at the 90° point. What does the AFH say?
options: He is right about medium banks, so the creep must come from the rudder: ease off the right rudder at the top to stop the bank growing
At the slow 90° point a slight amount of opposite aileron may be needed to stop overbanking, while he keeps rudder for the left-turning tendencies
Overbanking only appears past 45° of bank, so the creep means the roll-in was too fast; slow the roll and keep the ailerons neutral
Hold opposite aileron from the start of every climbing turn, because the lazy eight carries the steep turn's overbanking all the way around
questions.why: At the lazy eight's 90° point the bank reaches its maximum, about 30°, and the airspeed its minimum; in some flight conditions coordinated flight there needs a slight amount of opposite aileron to keep the wings from overbanking, while rudder pressure still cancels the left-turning tendencies [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. It is the effect he met in the chandelle, where the overbanking tendency increases as airspeed decreases [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. The medium-bank description, a bank that stays put with the aileron neutralized [[24:73|AFH 3-12]], does not cancel what slow speed does. Easing off the right rudder is wrong, since right rudder is applied at the apex in both turns [[24:216|AFH 10-7]], and the AFH asks for the aileron only near the 90° point, not all the way around.

questions.q: Your commercial learner asks, 'Which pulls more G, a steep turn or a lazy eight?' Which answer fits the sources?
options: In a level steep turn the bank alone sets it, 1.41 at 45° and 2.0 at 60°; in a lazy eight it depends on the speed of the dives and the abruptness of the pull-ups
The lazy eight always pulls more, because its top is flown 5 to 10 knots above stall and the load factor of any turn rises as the airspeed falls
They are the same: both reach about 30° of bank, and for a given bank the load factor is the same whether the turn is level, climbing or descending
The steep turn always pulls more, because a lazy eight never passes about 30° of bank and has no pull-up, so it can never pass about 1.15 G
questions.why: For a level turn the AFH says the same load factor always comes with a given bank, whatever the airspeed or airplane: 1.41 at 45° and 2.0 at 60° [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. For chandelles and lazy eights the PHAK says no definite statement is possible, because the load factor depends directly on the speed of the dives and the abruptness of the pull-ups; the better the maneuver is flown, the less extreme the load factor [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. A slow airplane is not a high-G airplane: the most load factor the wing can make varies with the square of the airspeed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. A steep turn is flown between 45° and 60° of bank [[24:210|AFH 10-1]], not 30°, and the lazy eight does have pull-ups.

questions.q: Your commercial learner flies good S-turns. In lazy eights she reaches each 180° point level at entry speed, then holds wings level for three seconds 'to reset, like crossing the road.' What do you tell her?
options: The pause is right in both: the ACS gives a short straight segment at each reversal so the pilot can check altitude and airspeed first
The pause is fine in lazy eights but not in S-turns, because a lazy eight is judged only on the numbers at each 180° point and never on its shape
Neither has a pause: S-turns roll straight into the opposite turn at the road, and a lazy eight starts the climbing turn the other way at once
Keep the pause but make it 5 seconds, the straight segment the AFH sets between pylons, so both loops start from the same heading
questions.why: The AFH compares the lazy eight to S-turns across a road, a 180° turn one way followed immediately by a 180° turn the other way [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. In S-turns the wings come level just as the airplane crosses the road, and there should be no delay before the next turn [[24:156|AFH 7-10]] (ACS AI.IX.E.S5). At a lazy eight's 180° point a climbing turn is started immediately in the opposite direction [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. The lazy eight is graded on shape too: the ACS wants the number of symmetrical loops specified (ACS AI.IX.D.S6), and a lack of symmetry is a listed error [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. The 3 to 5 seconds is the eights on pylons spacing between pylons [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

questions.q: As your learner, the examiner flies lazy eights with about 20° of bank at each 45° point, about 30° at each 90° point, matching loops, and every 180° point within tolerance. How do you treat the 20°?
options: As a failure of S5a, because the ACS requires 15° of bank at the 45° and 135° points, with a ±5° allowance, so 20° sits at the very edge
Not an ACS failure: the ACS grades about 30° at the steepest point, and 15° at 45° is the AFH sight picture; coach a slower roll if pitch suffers
As the error 'steep turn instead of a climbing maneuver,' which fails the Task outright whenever the bank at the 45° point passes 15°
As correct technique, because the AFH plans the bank at 45° as two-thirds of the maximum, so 20° and then 30° is exactly the intended picture
questions.why: The ACS bank element is approximately 30° at the steepest point (ACS AI.IX.D.S5a), which is the 90° point [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. The 15° at 45° comes from the AFH text: maximum pitch-up at the 45° point with an approximate bank of 15° [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. It is a planning picture, not an ACS line. The AFH also says why to watch it: the lazy eight should begin with a slow roll rate, because rising pitch plus rising bank can make the 45° point arrive before the highest pitch [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. 'Execution of a steep turn instead of a climbing maneuver' is a listed error [[24:216|AFH 10-7]], but no source ties it to a 15° figure, and no source sets two-thirds of anything.

questions.q: Your private learner flies a rectangular course with a strong wind on the tail of the downwind leg, the same setup she will meet in the traffic pattern. Which turn needs a relatively steep bank and more than 90° of heading change?
options: The base-to-upwind turn, because the headwind slows the airplane, and a slower airplane needs more bank and more heading change to turn the same corner
The downwind-to-base turn: groundspeed is highest as it starts, so the bank is relatively steep, and the crab on base makes the turn more than 90°
The upwind-to-crosswind turn, because the developing crosswind drifts the airplane into the course, which takes a steep, quick roll-in to stop
All four turns use the same bank and exactly 90°, because the course is a rectangle and the wind only affects the straight legs between turns
questions.why: The AFH: the turn from downwind to base is entered with a relatively steep bank because of the tailwind's groundspeed, and since the tailwind becomes a crosswind the pilot turns more than 90°, angling toward the inside of the course [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]. Base to upwind is a medium bank and less than 90°; upwind to crosswind is a slow, shallow roll-in because the crosswind drifts the airplane into the course, and less than 90° [[24:152|AFH 7-6]] [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]. The rule underneath is higher groundspeed, steeper bank [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]. The rectangular course exists to replicate the airport traffic pattern [[24:151|AFH 7-5]], which is why this downwind-to-base picture matters on a windy day.

questions.q: In S-turns you briefed that the wind needs a 10° wind correction angle at the 90° crosswind point. Your learner arrives there with the heading exactly 90° from where she crossed the road, and she starts to drift. Using the AFH example, how much heading change should the first 90° of ground track have taken?
options: 80°, because the wind correction angle is subtracted from the ground track whenever the airplane turns on the downwind side of the road
Exactly 90°: in a constant-radius turn the heading and the ground track always change by the same number of degrees, so her heading was right
About 100°: the heading must be 10° ahead of the track at the crosswind point, and the last 90° of track then takes only about 80°
About 110°, because the correction is applied twice, once for the drift and once for the change in groundspeed as the turn swings crosswind
questions.why: The AFH example: with a 10° wind correction angle needed when the airplane is directly crosswind, the heading is 10° ahead over the 90° point, so the first 90° of ground track takes 100° of heading change and the last 90° only 80° [[24:156|AFH 7-10]]. At the 90° point the airplane is directly crosswind and must have the correct wind correction angle [[24:155|AFH 7-9]]; with none, it drifts, which is the listed error 'failure to establish the appropriate wind correction angle' [[24:156|AFH 7-10]]. The ACS asks for adequate wind-drift correction to keep a constant radius on each side of the line (ACS AI.IX.E.S4). The air and the ground count turn degrees differently whenever there is wind [[24:156|AFH 7-10]].

questions.q: Your private learner wants to fly S-turns at 1,400 feet AGL 'for an extra safety margin.' Which reply fits the ACS and the AFH?
options: Fly them within the ACS entry band of 600 to 1,000 feet AGL, at a height where drift is easy to see from both sides and obstructions are cleared by 500 feet
Fine: the ACS sets only a lower limit for ground reference maneuvers, so any altitude above 600 feet AGL meets S3 as long as it is then held within ±100 feet throughout
Fine, but only for S-turns, because the 600 to 1,000 foot band in the ACS covers the rectangular course and turns around a point, not S-turns
Go higher still, to 1,500 feet AGL, because the steep spiral, chandelles and lazy eights all use that floor and the same safety rule applies here
questions.why: The ACS has S-turns entered perpendicular to the line at 600 to 1,000 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.E.S3b), and the same band appears for the rectangular course and turns around a point (ACS AI.IX.E.S3a, S3c). The AFH says ground reference maneuvers are generally flown there and lists what to weigh: drift should be easily recognizable from both sides, the lower the altitude the faster the airplane seems to move over the ground, obstructions need 500 feet vertical and 2,000 feet horizontal clearance, and lower altitude means less time and glide distance after an engine failure [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. The 1,500-foot AGL figure is the floor for the spiral, chandelle and lazy eight (ACS AI.IX.B.S6, AI.IX.C.S2, AI.IX.D.S2), not for this Task.

questions.q: A week before your ASEL CFI practical test, your study partner says, 'For Area IX we get one of steep turns or the spiral, one of chandelles or lazy eights, and one ground reference maneuver. Eights on pylons is optional.' What does the ACS really say?
options: At least three Tasks, one from each group, and eights on pylons is flown only if the evaluator still has time after the others
All six Tasks are always flown, and within the ground reference Task all three maneuvers must be demonstrated
At least four Tasks, including A or B, C or D, and both E and F; within Task E the evaluator picks at least one maneuver, so be ready for all three
At least four Tasks, but the applicant chooses which ones to fly and also chooses which of the three ground reference maneuvers to demonstrate within Task E
questions.why: For ASEL the evaluator must select at least four Area IX Tasks, including Task A or B, Task C or D, and Tasks E and F (ACS Area IX note). So the ground reference Task and eights on pylons are always on the list, and eights on pylons, the most advanced and difficult ground reference maneuver [[24:160|AFH 7-14]], is never optional. Inside Task E the evaluator selects at least one ground reference maneuver for the applicant to demonstrate (ACS AI.IX.E note): the rectangular course, S-turns or turns around a point (ACS AI.IX.E.S3). The evaluator, not the applicant, makes both choices.

questions.q: Fresh from turns around a point, your commercial learner flies his first eight on pylons at a constant altitude, steepening the bank downwind and shallowing it upwind to keep a perfect circle. The line wanders off the pylon all the way around. What do you teach?
options: His technique is right but the circle is too small: widen it until the bank changes are gentle, and the line will settle on the pylon by itself
Hold the bank constant and use rudder to keep the line on the pylon, because rudder is the finer control at low altitude and avoids bank changes
Eights on pylons needs no constant radius or drift correction in the turn: climb or descend with groundspeed so the line pivots on the pylon
Fly it as eights around pylons with a constant radius, then take the wind correction angle off the bank at each crosswind point to hold the line
questions.why: In turns around a point the pilot holds a constant radius by changing the bank with groundspeed [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]. Eights on pylons is different: the pilot holds a lateral relationship to the pylon, and the altitude is varied to keep the line on it [[24:160|AFH 7-14]] [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]. The maneuver does not require a constant radius, so no drift correction is applied in the turn; headed upwind the groundspeed and pivotal altitude drop, so the pilot descends [[24:163|AFH 7-17]], and the pivotal altitude varies through the turn with groundspeed [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. Using rudder to force the wing to the pylon puts the airplane in uncoordinated flight, low, in a steep bank, and should not be attempted [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

questions.q: Pylons are at 1,050 feet MSL and the crosswind groundspeed is 95 knots. Your learner computes her pivotal altitude, holds that altimeter number within 20 feet all the way around, and the line lags behind the pylon upwind and runs ahead of it downwind. What do you say?
options: Her 1,849-foot figure is only a starting point: groundspeed changes around the turn, so descend as the line lags upwind and climb as it runs ahead downwind
Her math is wrong: the 1,050 feet must be added twice, once for the pylon and once for the airplane's own height, so the target is about 2,900 feet MSL
Keep holding the altimeter number exactly; the line moves only because her bank is changing, and it is the bank, not the altitude, that sets the pivotal altitude
Climb as the line lags upwind and descend as it runs ahead downwind, because a higher altitude always speeds up the line's movement across the ground
questions.why: The rule of thumb: groundspeed squared divided by 11.3 for knots, plus the pylon's MSL elevation [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]: 95 x 95 = 9,025, / 11.3 = 799, + 1,050 = about 1,849 feet MSL. Pivotal altitude changes with groundspeed, so it varies through the turn and the pilot climbs or descends to hold the line [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. Upwind the groundspeed drops and so does the pivotal altitude, so she is too high there; a line moving behind the pylon means decrease altitude, and one moving ahead means increase it [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. The AFH says correcting pivotal altitude by the altimeter is ineffective, and the bank chosen does not alter the pivotal altitude [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

questions.q: On your CFI practical test the evaluator asks for turns around a point, then eights on pylons. Which statement about the two standards is correct?
options: Both hold altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots, and both share the AFH's 45° general bank limit, since both are ground reference maneuvers flown low
Turns around a point hold altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots; eights on pylons has no altitude tolerance, since altitude must change, and caps bank at 40°
Eights on pylons is held to ±100 feet of the computed pivotal altitude, while turns around a point allows any altitude change as long as the radius stays the same
Neither Task gives flight tolerances on the CFI test, because the applicant is graded only on the quality of the explanation and not on the flying itself
questions.why: The ground reference Task requires altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots (ACS AI.IX.E.S7). The eights on pylons Task has no altitude tolerance because the altitude is supposed to change with groundspeed [[24:162|AFH 7-16]], and its one number is a bank not to exceed 40° (ACS AI.IX.F.S5), tighter than the AFH's general 45° note for ground reference maneuvers [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. A computed pivotal altitude is only an estimate, and correcting it by the altimeter is ineffective [[24:163|AFH 7-17]], so a ±100-foot band around it makes no sense. The CFI applicant demonstrates and simultaneously explains, and both Tasks keep their flight elements (ACS AI.IX.E.S7, AI.IX.F.S5, S8).

questions.q: Your learner picks two lone trees for eights on pylons, on a line across the wind and about 4 seconds of straight flight apart. One stands in a creek bottom at 1,020 feet MSL, the other on a rise at 1,180 feet MSL. Crosswind groundspeed is 100 knots. What do you say?
options: Good choice: pivotal altitude is a height above the pylon, not above sea level, so one averaged altimeter target, about 1,985 feet MSL, works for both trees
Poor choice: the targets differ by 160 feet, about 1,905 and 2,065 feet MSL, so she would climb or descend between turns; pick pylons at one elevation
Fine, but turn around the higher tree first so the first turn is made into the wind at the higher pivotal altitude
The trees are too close together: the AFH wants about 10 seconds between pylons so the altitude change can be made in level flight
questions.why: Rule of thumb: groundspeed squared divided by 11.3 for knots, plus the MSL elevation of the pylon [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]: 100 x 100 = 10,000, / 11.3 = 885 feet, so about 1,905 feet MSL over the first tree and 2,065 feet MSL over the second, 160 feet apart. The AFH wants pylons at the same elevation, since differences of over a few feet mean climbing or descending between each turn [[24:162|AFH 7-16]], and poor choice of pylons is a listed error [[24:164|AFH 7-18]]. Spacing of 3 to 5 seconds and a line perpendicular to the wind are exactly what the AFH asks for [[24:162|AFH 7-16]], so those parts were right. An averaged number fits neither tree.
